name: Shirley Temple
description: Ginger ale with grenadine and a cherry. The first drink most people are ever served in a glass that looks grown up.
funFact: Shirley Temple herself disliked it and said so repeatedly, calling it too sweet, and never received a cent from the restaurants that sold it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the ginger ale.
Pour the grenadine down the inside of the glass so it settles at the bottom.
Drop in a cherry and serve without stirring.

name: Roy Rogers
description: Cola with grenadine and a cherry. The Shirley Temple for whoever did not want the ginger ale.
funFact: The pair were named for two film stars of the same era and served side by side, which made ordering one of them a small declaration of taste.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the cola.
Pour the grenadine slowly down the side.
Drop in a cherry and serve.

name: Arnold Palmer
description: Iced tea and lemonade, half and half. Named for a golfer who ordered it so often that bar staff learned the ratio.
funFact: Palmer ordered it at a Palm Springs restaurant loudly enough that a woman at the next table asked for the same, and the name stuck that afternoon.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour the iced tea and lemonade in together.
Stir once to combine.
Hang a lemon wheel on the rim.

name: Virgin Mary
description: A Bloody Mary with the vodka left out, which changes almost nothing about how it is made.
funFact: The seasoning does all the work in a Bloody Mary, which is why the alcohol-free version is one of the very few that loses nothing at all.

steps: Combine everything but the ice and roll it between two tins to mix without foaming.
Pour into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Season the top with more celery salt and cracked pepper.
Garnish with a celery stick and a lemon wedge.
recipe.garnish: A celery stick and a lemon wedge

name: Cinderella
description: Pineapple, orange and lemon shaken hard and topped with soda. The Savoy's own alcohol-free drink.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book prints a short run of temperance drinks alongside 750 alcoholic ones, and this is the only one that has stayed in print.

steps: Shake the three juices and the grenadine hard with ice.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Top with soda water.
Garnish with orange and a cherry.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cherry

name: Egg Cream
description: Milk, seltzer and chocolate syrup, containing neither egg nor cream. The Brooklyn candy-store drink.
funFact: The name has never been explained convincingly; the drink has no egg and no cream, and Brooklyn has been arguing about why for a hundred years.

steps: Pour the milk into a tall glass.
Spray the seltzer in hard, straight down, to raise a thick white head.
Slide the chocolate syrup down the inside of the glass under the foam.
Stir the bottom only, leaving the white head intact, and drink it immediately.
recipe.garnish: None — the white head is the drink

name: Italian Soda
description: Flavoured syrup, soda water and ice. Add cream and it becomes a French soda, which is the only difference.
funFact: It is not Italian — the name came from American coffee bars in the 1980s selling Italian-branded syrups, and no bar in Italy calls it that.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour the syrup over the ice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once, or float a spoon of cream on top to make it a French soda.

name: Agua de Jamaica
description: Dried hibiscus steeped and sweetened, served ice cold. Deep red, sharply tart, and sold on every Mexican corner.
funFact: The flowers are calyces rather than petals, and the same plant travels the world under different names — sorrel in the Caribbean, karkade in Egypt, bissap in Senegal.

steps: Boil half the water and pour it over the hibiscus. Steep for 20 minutes.
Strain, pressing the flowers, and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the remaining cold water and the lime juice.
Chill thoroughly and serve over plenty of ice.

name: Horchata
description: Rice steeped with cinnamon, blended and strained into a cold sweet white drink.
funFact: Spain's original is made from tigernuts rather than rice — horchata de chufa — and the two versions share a name, a colour and almost nothing else.

steps: Soak the rice and cinnamon in the water overnight.
Blend the whole lot until the rice breaks down completely.
Strain twice through a fine cloth until no grit remains.
Stir in the milk, sugar and vanilla, chill hard and serve over ice.

name: Tamarindo
description: Tamarind pulp, sugar and water. Sour, brown and far more refreshing than it looks.
funFact: Tamarind reached Mexico from Asia by way of the Manila galleons, and stayed so thoroughly that it now reads as a Mexican flavour rather than an imported one.

steps: Shell the pods and simmer the pulp in half the water until it softens.
Mash and push it through a sieve, discarding the seeds and fibres.
Stir in the sugar and the remaining cold water.
Chill and serve over ice with a pinch of salt if you like it sharper.

name: Atole
description: Masa cooked into hot milk with cinnamon and sugar. Thick enough to be breakfast, and drunk from a mug.
funFact: Atole predates the Spanish arrival by centuries and is one of very few pre-Columbian drinks still made the same way in the same country.

steps: Whisk the masa into the cold water until completely smooth with no lumps.
Heat the milk with the cinnamon and piloncillo until the sugar dissolves.
Pour in the masa mixture in a steady stream, whisking constantly.
Simmer gently for ten minutes, stirring, until it thickens. Add the vanilla and serve hot.

name: Champurrado
description: Atole with Mexican chocolate whisked through it. Thicker, darker, and the one that goes with tamales.
funFact: Mexican drinking chocolate is deliberately gritty — the sugar is coarse and unrefined, and the texture is the point rather than a flaw to be smoothed out.

steps: Whisk the masa into the cold water until smooth.
Heat the milk with the chocolate, piloncillo and cinnamon until melted.
Whisk hard with a molinillo or a balloon whisk until it foams.
Stir in the masa mixture and simmer, stirring, until thick. Serve very hot.

name: Ponche Navideño
description: Hot fruit punch with tejocotes, guava, sugarcane and hibiscus. Mexican Christmas in a clay mug.
funFact: The fruit is meant to be eaten out of the bottom of the mug with a spoon, which is why it is served in a wide clay jarrito rather than a glass.

steps: Simmer the water with the piloncillo, cinnamon and sugarcane for 20 minutes.
Add the tejocotes and prunes and simmer another 20 minutes until soft.
Add the guava and hibiscus and simmer for a final 15 minutes.
Ladle into clay mugs, making sure each one gets fruit, and serve very hot.
recipe.garnish: The fruit itself, in the bottom of the mug

name: Morir Soñando
description: Orange juice and cold milk beaten together with sugar and ice. The name means to die dreaming.
funFact: Everything has to be properly cold before it meets — warm juice curdles the milk instantly, and the whole technique is about avoiding that.

steps: Stir the sugar into the cold milk until fully dissolved.
Fill a tall glass with ice and pour the milk over it to chill it further.
Add the cold orange juice in a slow stream while stirring constantly.
Serve at once, before it has any chance to separate.

name: Chicha Morada
description: Purple corn boiled with pineapple, apple and spice, then cooled and sharpened with lime.
funFact: Peruvian purple corn is one of the most anthocyanin-rich foods known, which is why the drink comes out an almost unnatural violet.

steps: Boil the corn with the pineapple rind, apple, cloves and cinnamon for 45 minutes.
Strain and discard the solids.
Stir in the sugar while the liquid is still warm.
Cool completely, then add the lime juice and serve over ice with diced apple.
recipe.garnish: Diced apple and a lime wheel

name: Mauby
description: Mauby bark boiled with spice and sweetened. Bitter in a way no other soft drink is, and drunk for exactly that.
funFact: The bitterness comes from the bark of Colubrina elliptica and lingers long after swallowing — Barbadians describe acquiring the taste as a rite of passage.

steps: Boil the bark with the spices in the water for 30 minutes.
Strain and stir in the sugar while hot.
Cool completely — it turns more bitter as it cools, which is expected.
Dilute to taste with cold water and serve over plenty of ice.

name: Colada Morada
description: Purple corn flour cooked with berries, spice and herbs. Ecuador drinks it once a year, for the dead.
funFact: It is served on the second of November with guaguas de pan — bread shaped as swaddled infants — and the pairing is not optional.

steps: Simmer the water with the panela, spices and lemongrass for 30 minutes, then strain.
Blend and sieve the berries, and add the purée to the spiced liquid.
Whisk the corn flour into a little cold water and stir it in.
Simmer, stirring constantly, until it thickens. Add the pineapple at the end and serve hot.

name: Ayran
description: Yoghurt whisked with cold water and salt. Savoury rather than sweet, and drunk with grilled meat.
funFact: Turkey sells more ayran than cola, and it is the drink poured alongside kebab everywhere from roadside grills to the state airline.

steps: Whisk the yoghurt and salt together until completely smooth.
Add the cold water in a stream, whisking, until it is drinkable and slightly frothy.
Pour over ice.
Serve at once, before the froth falls.
recipe.garnish: A dried mint dusting, in some regions

name: Doogh
description: Yoghurt thinned with sparkling water and seasoned with dried mint. Ayran's sharper Persian cousin.
funFact: The carbonation is the difference — Persian doogh is traditionally naturally fizzy from a brief fermentation, which soda water now imitates.

steps: Whisk the yoghurt, salt and dried mint until smooth.
Add the sparkling water slowly so it keeps its bubble.
Pour over ice without stirring hard.
Dust with more dried mint and serve.
recipe.garnish: Dried mint and a cucumber slice

name: Sekanjabin
description: Mint and vinegar syrup diluted with cold water. Sweet and sour at once, and a thousand years old.
funFact: It is the ancestor of the shrub — the drinking-vinegar tradition reached Europe through Persian and Arab medicine, and the word sherbet comes along the same route.

steps: Simmer the sugar and water until it forms a light syrup.
Add the vinegar and simmer for another 15 minutes.
Take it off the heat, drop in the mint, and leave to steep until cool. Strain and bottle.
To serve, dilute one part syrup to five parts cold water, over ice, with grated cucumber.
recipe.garnish: Grated cucumber and a mint sprig

name: Jallab
description: Date and grape molasses with rose water, poured over crushed ice and topped with pine nuts and raisins.
funFact: The syrup is traditionally smoked with Arabic incense before bottling, which is where the faint resinous note underneath the sweetness comes from.

steps: Soak the pine nuts and raisins in cold water for an hour so they soften and float.
Stir the syrup and rose water into the cold water until fully combined.
Fill a tall glass with crushed ice and pour the mixture over.
Spoon the soaked pine nuts and raisins on top.

name: Salep
description: Hot milk thickened with orchid tuber flour and dusted with cinnamon. Drunk from a cup on winter streets in Istanbul.
funFact: Real salep flour is milled from wild orchid tubers, and harvesting has been restricted for decades — most street salep today is a starch blend by necessity.

steps: Whisk the salep flour and sugar into the cold milk before any heat goes near it.
Heat slowly, whisking constantly, so it thickens without catching.
Simmer for five minutes until it coats the back of a spoon.
Pour into cups and dust heavily with cinnamon.

name: Boza
description: Fermented millet, thick and faintly sour, served cold with cinnamon and roasted chickpeas.
funFact: Vefa Bozacısı has sold it from the same Istanbul shop since 1876, and still keeps the glass Atatürk drank from on display.

steps: Boil the grain in the water until it collapses completely, then blend and sieve it smooth.
Stir in the sugar and cool to room temperature.
Add the starter and leave, covered, for a day or two until it turns faintly sour and fizzy.
Chill and serve in cups, dusted with cinnamon and scattered with roasted chickpeas.

name: Lassi
description: Yoghurt blended with water and sugar until frothy. The sweet version of a drink that is just as often salted.
funFact: Salted lassi came first and remains the everyday one across much of northern India; sweet lassi is the version that travelled.

steps: Blend the yoghurt, water and sugar until light and frothy.
Add the cardamom and blend again briefly.
Pour over ice into a tall glass.
Top with a spoon of the froth from the blender.
recipe.garnish: Ground cardamom and a pistachio dusting

name: Mango Lassi
description: Lassi made with ripe mango pulp. Thicker, sweeter, and the version most of the world met first.
funFact: Alphonso mangoes are the ones worth using and are in season for barely two months, which is why tinned Alphonso pulp is a legitimate ingredient rather than a compromise.

steps: Blend the mango, yoghurt, milk and sugar until completely smooth.
Taste and add sugar only if the mango needs it.
Pour over ice.
Dust with cardamom and chopped pistachio.

name: Falooda
description: Rose syrup, milk, vermicelli, basil seeds and ice cream in one tall glass. Drink and dessert at once.
funFact: Basil seeds swell into translucent jelly in water within minutes, and that texture — not the flavour, which is negligible — is the entire reason they are in the glass.

steps: Soak the basil seeds in water for 20 minutes until they swell and turn translucent.
Spoon the rose syrup into the bottom of a tall glass, then the vermicelli and basil seeds.
Pour the cold milk over slowly so the layers stay visible.
Top with a scoop of ice cream and scatter chopped nuts over it.
recipe.garnish: Chopped pistachio and a rose petal

name: Teh Tarik
description: Strong tea and condensed milk poured between two vessels from arm's length until it foams.
funFact: Tarik means pulled — the long pour aerates the tea and cools it, and the height of the pull is a genuine point of pride among stall owners.

steps: Brew the tea strong and strain it.
Stir in the condensed and evaporated milk until dissolved.
Pour it back and forth between two jugs, pulling the stream as far apart as you dare.
Stop when a thick head of foam has built, and serve immediately.

name: Cendol
description: Green rice-flour jellies in coconut milk and palm sugar syrup over shaved ice.
funFact: The green comes from pandan leaf rather than food colouring, and the jellies are pressed through a perforated mould straight into iced water to set.

steps: Pile shaved ice into a bowl or a wide glass.
Spoon the green cendol jellies over the ice.
Pour the salted coconut milk over the top.
Finish with a heavy drizzle of palm sugar syrup and stir before eating.
recipe.garnish: A drizzle of palm sugar syrup

name: Es Kelapa Muda
description: Young coconut water and its soft flesh over ice with palm sugar. Served in the shell it came out of.
funFact: The flesh of a young coconut is soft enough to scrape out with a spoon and is nothing like the hard white meat of a mature one.

steps: Open the coconut at the top and pour the water into a jug.
Scrape the soft flesh out in strips with a spoon.
Stir the palm sugar syrup and lime into the water.
Return everything to the shell with ice, and serve with a spoon and a straw.

name: Nam Manao
description: Lime juice, sugar and salt over crushed ice. Three ingredients and the salt is not optional.
funFact: The pinch of salt is what makes it Thai — it flattens the sharp edge of the lime and makes the drink read as balanced rather than sour.

steps: Stir the lime juice, syrup and salt together until the salt dissolves.
Add the cold water.
Fill a tall glass with crushed ice and pour over.
Stir once and taste — it should be sour first, then sweet, then faintly salty.

name: Suanmeitang
description: Smoked sour plums boiled with hawthorn and osmanthus. Dark, tart and drunk cold all summer.
funFact: It was an imperial court drink under the Qing, and Beijing families still boil a pot at the start of summer and keep it in the fridge until autumn.

steps: Rinse the plums and hawthorn and soak them for an hour.
Boil everything but the osmanthus and sugar for 45 minutes.
Add the rock sugar and osmanthus and simmer for a final five minutes.
Strain, cool completely and serve very cold over ice.

name: Sujeonggwa
description: Cinnamon and ginger boiled separately then combined, sweetened, and served cold with persimmon and pine nuts.
funFact: The cinnamon and ginger are boiled in separate pots and only combined at the end, because cooking them together muddies both.

steps: Boil the cinnamon in half the water and the ginger in the other half, separately, for 40 minutes each.
Strain both and combine, then stir in the sugar and simmer until dissolved.
Cool completely and refrigerate overnight.
Serve very cold with a soaked dried persimmon and a few pine nuts floating on top.

name: Sikhye
description: Sweet rice punch with the grains left floating. Malted, faintly grainy and served ice cold after a meal.
funFact: The malt enzymes convert the rice starch to sugar — the same process that starts a beer, halted before any fermentation can begin.

steps: Steep the malt powder in the water for an hour, then strain and keep the clear liquid.
Add the cooked rice and hold at 60C for four to five hours until the grains float.
Skim off the floating rice and reserve it, then boil the liquid with the sugar and ginger.
Cool completely and serve very cold with a spoonful of the reserved rice and a few pine nuts.
recipe.garnish: Floating rice grains and pine nuts

name: Amazake
description: Rice fermented with koji into a thick sweet drink. No sugar is added and none is needed.
funFact: All the sweetness comes from koji enzymes breaking rice starch into glucose — the same mould that starts sake, stopped before yeast is ever introduced.

steps: Cool the cooked rice to about 60C and stir the koji and water through it.
Hold it at 55 to 60C for eight to ten hours, stirring occasionally.
Taste — it is done when it is properly sweet with no starchiness left.
Thin with hot water to drink, and serve with a little grated ginger.

name: Calpis
description: Cultured milk concentrate diluted with cold water. Tart, milky and unlike anything outside Japan.
funFact: It has been made since 1919 and is sold abroad as Calpico, because the original name lands badly in English for reasons the company worked out late.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour the concentrate over.
Add cold water — roughly four parts to one — and stir.
Use soda water instead for Calpis Soda.

name: Ramune
description: Lemon-lime soda sealed by a glass marble that you punch into the neck to open.
funFact: The Codd-neck bottle is held shut by its own carbonation pressing a marble against a rubber seal, and the marble stays rattling in the neck for the rest of the drink.

steps: Chill the bottle thoroughly — it will foam over if it is warm.
Peel the wrapper and fit the plastic plunger into the top.
Push down hard and fast to drive the marble into the neck.
Hold it upright for a moment while it foams, then drink from the bottle.
recipe.garnish: None — the marble is the point

name: Barley Water
description: Barley boiled with lemon peel and sugar, strained and served cold. Wimbledon has poured it since 1935.
funFact: Robinsons has been the Wimbledon barley water since 1935, when it was first sold there as a drink for players rather than spectators.

steps: Rinse the barley, cover with the water and simmer for 30 minutes.
Add the lemon peel and simmer another 10 minutes.
Strain, stir in the sugar and lemon juice while still hot, and discard the barley.
Cool completely and serve over ice.

name: Kompot
description: Fruit simmered in water with a little sugar and served cold. Every Polish household makes it and none the same way.
funFact: It is what happens to fruit that is too ripe to keep, which is why the recipe is different in every kitchen and formalised in none of them.

steps: Put the fruit, sugar and spices in a pot with the water.
Bring to a boil, then simmer for 20 minutes until the fruit gives up its colour.
Take it off the heat and leave it to cool with the fruit still in.
Strain or don't, chill, and serve cold with a few pieces of the fruit in the glass.
recipe.garnish: A few pieces of the cooked fruit

name: Switchel
description: Water, cider vinegar, ginger and molasses. What American farmhands drank in the hayfield before anyone sold sports drinks.
funFact: It was known as haymaker's punch and drunk warm as often as cold, on the reasoning that a cold drink in the heat was dangerous.

steps: Whisk the vinegar, molasses and grated ginger together until smooth.
Add the cold water and stir well.
Let it sit for an hour so the ginger infuses, then strain.
Serve over ice, or warm on a cold day as it was originally drunk.

name: Shrub
description: Drinking vinegar cut with soda. A colonial way of keeping fruit that turned out to be a good drink.
funFact: Vinegar preserves the fruit and the sugar preserves the vinegar, which is why a shrub keeps for a year without refrigeration and why colonial households made it by the gallon.

steps: Mash the fruit with the sugar and leave it, covered, for two days until it releases its syrup.
Strain, pressing the fruit, then stir in the vinegar. Bottle it and leave a week to mellow.
To serve, pour one ounce of shrub over ice.
Top with soda water and stir once.

name: Sarsaparilla
description: Root-brewed soda with a medicinal edge. The drink that root beer came from and then left behind.
funFact: It was sold as a blood purifier in nineteenth-century pharmacies, and the flavour still reads as medicine to anyone who did not grow up with it.

steps: Simmer the roots in the water for 30 minutes.
Strain and stir in the sugar and vanilla while hot.
Cool completely — this is the syrup, and it keeps for weeks.
Serve one part syrup to four parts soda water, over plenty of ice.

name: Root Beer
description: Sassafras, wintergreen and vanilla brewed into a foaming soda. Deeply American and baffling everywhere else.
funFact: Safrole, the compound that gave real sassafras its flavour, was banned by the FDA in 1960 — every root beer since uses safrole-free extract.

steps: Dissolve the sugar in warm water and stir in the extract and vanilla.
Cool completely to make the syrup.
Mix one part syrup to four parts cold soda water.
Serve in a mug that has been in the freezer, which is not optional.
recipe.garnish: None — a frosted mug is the whole presentation

name: Birch Beer
description: Birch bark soda, sharper and more minty than root beer. Comes red, brown or clear depending on the county.
funFact: Pennsylvania Dutch country takes the colour seriously — red birch beer and white birch beer are different drinks there, and people hold opinions.

steps: Simmer the birch bark in the water for 30 minutes.
Strain and stir in the sugar and wintergreen while hot.
Cool completely to make the syrup.
Serve one part syrup to four parts soda water over ice, in a frosted mug.

name: Champola
description: Soursop pulp blended with milk and sugar. Cuba's answer to a milkshake, made from a fruit that tastes faintly of pineapple.
funFact: Soursop flesh has to be pulled apart and the seeds picked out by hand — they are mildly toxic and never go in the blender.

steps: Pull the soursop flesh apart by hand and remove every seed.
Blend the pulp with the milk, sugar and vanilla until smooth.
Add ice and blend again briefly.
Pour into a tall glass and serve at once.

name: Batido
description: Tropical fruit blended with ice and a little water or milk. The everyday drink of a Venezuelan lunch counter.
funFact: A batido made with water is called a batido de agua and one with milk a merengada, and ordering the wrong one gets you a different drink entirely.

steps: Put the fruit, liquid, sugar and lime in a blender.
Add the ice and blend until smooth and thick.
Taste and adjust — ripe fruit often needs no sugar at all.
Pour into a tall glass and drink cold.
recipe.garnish: A wedge of the fruit used
